title: Bouncy gospel singing and her first songs
summary: She moved from Apollo to Columbia, says she started bouncy gospel by singing like the congregation, and recalls Daniel Saw the Stone.

I sing the, uh, I sing a lot of the late American, late ballads they got out, like, I Believe and, uh, His Hands. And that's one of my late records on Columbia. I'm now with Columbia records. I was with Apollo for 10 years. Of course, I had a record there that opened the doors for me to the, to, to, to make these big concerts. It was an old time spiritual that I revived with the bounce. Gospel singing just started to having this bounce. And I, uh, was the first one to start this bouncy gospel singing. You know, it was just like a lot of dead music. They used to sing it like everybody was dying or somebody going to a funeral. But, uh, that's when the choir master would sing it. But I always found out that in church service, that the, the convocation or the congregation would always be more jolly and sound better than the choir. That's probably true. Yeah. Yeah. That's because people sing the way it come out of their heart. And the choir always sound dead because the choir director, the person who wrote the music, took all the feeling out of it and made it scientific instead of making it real. And so I, I didn't like the way the choir sang. And so I start to sing it the way I hear the people singing in the congregation in the church around the home. And, of course, leaving the South, coming to Chicago, I started that type of singing. And many people that had left the South, they were living in Chicago. When they heard that type of singing, it was the type that they liked. And that's how I got popular and spread it all over.
Which were your first songs? The ones that really made you famous?

The ones that I came up from New Orleans with. We started to sing an old song about Daniel saw the stone. Now you might hear a choir singing, and they'll sing it so it's with a lot of opera tones to it, you know. But I didn't. I'd sing it, just went on. Oh, Daniel saw the stone that was you'd up to mountain, you'd up to mountain, you'd up to mountain, you'd up to mountain. Daniel saw the stone that was you'd up to mountain, came down to redeem a mighty world. And then it was simple, and the people could catch on. I'd start singing, and everybody in the church. Oh, Daniel saw the stone that was you'd up to mountain, you'd up to mountain. And then the tenor and the sopranos, and all, you know, nobody had, no choir director had to say, now the tenor sang this, the alto sang that, and the bass sang this. They're always bass together without any training, and they come out of their heart. It must be wonderful to sing with that spontaneity. Yeah, I don't like to be, you know, so, so, form. I like to relax myself. And right now, if we start to sing it right now, I bet you the people would come up. And you wouldn't have to tell them what voice to sing it, because their voice would automatically blend in.

But you know, something happened to me while we were talking. Something, this seems to be contagious, you see, this kind of life.
